correctness.rationale: For an integer diagonal gain q, integration of a test function of {q u+s} over u is the same as integration against uniform measure. Iterating this partial integration in x, then y, then z proves product Lebesgue invariance in the frozen modulus-one, fixed-translation setting. In the phase covariance, write u=(j+v)/q: summing j leaves 1/q times the unit-gain correlation. Splitting v at 1-{s} gives (1/12-{s}(1-{s})/2)/q=B_2({s})/(2q). The independent uniform forcing coordinate and even periodic B_2 give the stated absolute-amplitude dependence and factors 1/(2a), 1/(2c). The low-amplitude quadratic is (B-5/6)^2/5+1/36, including B=0 and B=1 up to a null endpoint. For B>=1, put K(B)=2 sqrt(B) J(B). Its first full period is 1/15; on each later full period twice integrating by parts gives a strictly positive integral because H(u)=u^2(1-u)^2/12 has H''=B_2 and both H and H' vanish at the endpoints, while the weight has positive second derivative. The possible final fragment subtracts at most sqrt(3)/(54 sqrt(k)) for k=floor(B)>=1, by integrating the negative part of (u-1/2)^2-1/12. This cannot erase 1/15. At infinity, the periodic primitive of the mean-zero B_2 is bounded, so the improper integral tail is O(B^(-1/2)). For the Fourier series one may integrate on finite intervals using absolute uniform summability and then take the limit: each frequency k has a tail bound O(1/(k sqrt(B))) by integration by parts. The Fresnel integral is 1/(2 sqrt(k)), giving K(infinity)=zeta(5/2)/(2 pi^2) and J(B)=zeta(5/2)/(4 pi^2 sqrt(B))+O(B^(-1)). The absolute convergence used is that of the Fourier series, not the unweighted-sign improper integral of absolute values. The frozen RESULT.md lines 34–76 give the analytic replay path. VERIFICATION.md and verify.py were inspected, not executed; finite diagnostics are not needed to establish the global sign or limit.
